strengths: Addresses a novel and timely problem: image knowledge copyright protection in multimodal RAG-as-a-Service, which is indeed underexplored compared to text-only RAG watermarking.

Two complementary watermarking strategies (acronym-based and spatial-relationship-based) are well-motivated by differing OCR/spatial reasoning capabilities across VLMs, providing some flexibility for black-box deployment.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two datasets (MMQA, WebQA) and four VLM generators (LLaVA-NeXT, InternVL3, Qwen-VL-Chat, Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct), covering effectiveness, harmlessness, stealthiness, and robustness.
Statistical verification framework using Welch's t-test and clearly defined metrics (Rank, CGSR, VSR, SimScore) gives a rigorous quantitative basis for watermark detection claims.

Robustness tests against common image transformations (rescale, rotate, Gaussian blur) and query-efficiency comparison against baselines (Naive, Opt.) show the method requires fewer queries to reach statistical significance.

Ablation-style experiments (PCA visualization, retrieval ratio vs. watermark number, relevant-query harmlessness tests) add useful supporting evidence to the paper's stealthiness and harmlessness claims.
weaknesses: The core watermarking techniques are conceptually simple (embedding an OCR-readable text string or an unusual spatial arrangement into a synthetic image), which is a fairly straightforward extension of existing text/image generation tools rather than a fundamentally new watermarking mechanism; novelty is more in the application/combination than in the underlying technique.

Stealthiness claims rely mainly on embedding-space similarity (PCA, low unintended retrieval rate) but do not address a natural and simple adversarial defense: an adversary could run OCR or object-anomaly detectors over the knowledge base to flag/filter images containing suspicious embedded text (AQUA_acronym) or implausible scene compositions (AQUA_spatial), which seems like an easy and effective countermeasure that is not evaluated.

Robustness evaluation is limited to generic image transformations (rescale, rotate, Gaussian blur) and does not test targeted removal attacks specifically designed against the watermark signal (e.g., text-region inpainting/cropping for acronym watermarks, or object removal/replacement for spatial watermarks).

The reference distribution values used for real-world deployment (Appendix B) appear to be fixed illustrative numbers rather than derived systematically, raising questions about how practical and generalizable the proposed real-world verification protocol actually is.

The method and evaluation are restricted to the T2T (text-to-text) multimodal RAG subclass; generalization to other multimodal RAG architectures (e.g., text-and-image-to-image) is left entirely to future work, limiting the scope of the contribution.

The threat model assumes the defender can freely craft arbitrary secret acronyms/spatial scenes and that the adversary does not attempt any content sanitization or moderation of ingested data, which may be optimistic relative to real RaaS deployments that often include content filtering.

Limited discussion of watermark scalability and quality control when generating large numbers of watermark images via LLM/diffusion pipelines, including potential collisions, low-quality generations, or detectability patterns that might emerge at scale.

No comparison to more sophisticated or recent watermarking baselines beyond the two self-constructed baselines (Naive and PGD-based Opt.), which may not represent the strongest possible adversarial detection or attack scenario.

strengths: Addresses a novel and practical problem: no prior work watermarks image knowledge in Multimodal RAG-as-a-Service, filling a clear gap relative to text-only RAG watermarking methods.

Two complementary, well-motivated watermarking mechanisms (acronym-based OCR triggers and spatial-relationship cues) that are designed to survive indirect (image-to-text) watermark propagation, a genuinely distinct challenge from prior image watermarking or text RAG watermarking.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 4 generator VLMs, 2 datasets, and multiple model scales (2B-38B), with principled statistical verification (Welch's t-test, Z-test, hypothesis testing framework) rather than only point-estimate detection rates.

Thorough coverage of all four stated design goals (effectiveness, harmlessness, stealthiness, robustness), including PCA stealthiness analysis, adaptive VLM-based filtering adversaries, WAVES-benchmark image transformation/regeneration attacks, retriever replacement/fine-tuning, corpus scaling, and adversarial fine-tuning to suppress watermark responses.
Reasonable baselines (naive common-image watermark and PGD-based optimization watermark) that highlight AQUA's superior query efficiency and detection reliability.
Good reproducibility support: code released, public datasets used, detailed appendices with prompts, hyperparameters, and additional qualitative examples.

Practical discussion of real-world deployment issues (reference distribution estimation, multi-provider watermark collision avoidance) that shows awareness of deployment realism beyond a narrow lab setting.
weaknesses: The threat model assumes the defender can freely inject synthetic watermark images into a proprietary dataset and craft arbitrary probe queries with known ground-truth signatures; whether real data providers would accept modifying their datasets with fabricated images is not deeply discussed, and could raise questions about knowledge-base integrity/utility beyond the tested QA benchmarks.

AQUA_acronym and AQUA_spatial both rely on model capabilities (OCR and spatial/compositional reasoning) that could vary substantially across future or non-English VLMs; generalization to weaker or specialized (e.g., domain-specific, non-VLM) RAG generators is not evaluated.

The 'Opt.' PGD baseline is a somewhat weak/non-specialized comparator for this setting (imperceptible adversarial perturbation baselines are typically designed for classification, not VLM instruction following), so the large performance gap over baselines may partly reflect baseline mismatch rather than purely AQUA's advantage.

Stealthiness claims rest partly on PCA visualization and VLM-filter FPR/TPR trade-offs; a human perceptual study or more rigorous statistical distinguishability test (beyond PCA and a single VLM filter) is absent, leaving open whether sophisticated or multimodal forensic detectors could still discriminate watermark images.

The spatial method’s reliance on 'improbable scenes' (e.g., apple on a dog's head) could, in principle, be noticeable to human curators or downstream users even if VLM filters struggle, and this human-in-the-loop risk is not empirically tested.

Watermark collision avoidance across multiple data providers is discussed only qualitatively/theoretically (Appendix B.2) without empirical validation of the proposed centralized registry or combinatorial verification claims.

Robustness experiments use attack 'strength' fixed at 1 in the WAVES benchmark; it is unclear how AQUA performs under stronger degradations or more adaptive attacks that specifically target the geometric/semantic cues (e.g., object removal or scene rearrangement attacks tailored to spatial watermarks).
